details:
**2.5 percent**
The standard rate of zakat: Muslims give 2.5% (one-fortieth) of qualifying wealth, such as savings, gold, silver, and trade goods, that they have held for a full lunar year. This figure is the most common giveaway clue.

**Third Pillar of Islam**
Zakat, or obligatory almsgiving, is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It is usually counted third, after the shahadah (declaration of faith) and salat (prayer) and before sawm (fasting during Ramadan) and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).

**Nisab**
The minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must own before zakat becomes mandatory. It is traditionally set by a value in gold or silver, so only those above the threshold are required to pay.

**Sadaqah**
Voluntary charity in Islam, which can be given at any time and in any amount. It is contrasted with zakat, which is obligatory and fixed in rate.

**Zakat al-Fitr (Sadaqat al-Fitr, fitrana)**
A special form of zakat paid at the end of Ramadan, before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, so the poor can also celebrate. Based on a hadith narrated by Ibn Umar, it is set at one sa' (a measure of volume) of a staple food such as dates or barley per household member.

**Asnaf (eight categories of recipients)**
The eligible recipients of zakat, listed in Quran 9:60. They are the poor, the needy, zakat collectors, those whose hearts are to be reconciled (such as new converts), slaves being freed, debtors, those "in the cause of God" (fi sabilillah), and travelers.

**Fi sabilillah**
"In the path of God," one of the eight categories of zakat recipients. Scholars dispute whether it refers only to funding jihad and fighters or more broadly to any charitable cause that serves God.

**Ridda Wars**
The "Wars of Apostasy" (632–633) fought by the first caliph Abu Bakr after Muhammad's death. Several Arabian tribes rejected Muslim authority, and some refused to pay zakat to Medina; Abu Bakr treated this refusal as rebellion.

**Amil**
The officials who collect and distribute zakat when it is administered by the state. Collectors are themselves one of the eight eligible categories of recipients, so they may be paid from zakat funds.

**Zia ul-Haq and ushr**
Pakistan's military ruler Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq made zakat and ushr compulsory in 1980 as part of his Islamization program, run through government zakat councils and local committees. Ushr is a tithe on agricultural produce.

**Descendants of the Prophet excluded**
Muhammad's family, the Banu Hashim and their descendants (Sayyids), are traditionally forbidden from receiving zakat. It is considered the "impurity" of people's wealth and unfit for the Prophet's household.

**Tzedakah and dana (almsgiving in other religions)**
Zakat is often compared with charity in other faiths: tzedakah in Judaism ("righteousness"), for which Maimonides ranked eight levels of giving, and dana (generosity) in Buddhism. Christian almsgiving clues include Jesus's teaching in Matthew not to let the left hand know what the right hand is doing and the parable of the widow's two mites.
